newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE suspends voter registration in Bosnian town.
newsitem.headline: OSCE suspends voter registration in Bosnian town.

text.p: The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said on Wednesday it had shut down voter registration centres in the disputed Bosnian town of Brcko due to reports that Serb authorities were orchestrating widespread fraud.
International election supervisors reported voters were presenting suspicious documents when registering for local polls in the Serb-controlled town, OSCE spokesman David Foley said.

"We're closing all four voter registration centres in Brcko because reports from OSCE personnel presented evidence that there may be pervasive violations of rules and regulations regarding voter registration," Foley said.
"Further measures are being decided on today, but it is likely that there will be a complete re-registration of all those who registered in four registration centres in Brcko," he said.
Bosnian Serb and Moslem-Croat authorities view the municipal elections in September as a battle for control over territory contested during the 1992-95 war, particularly in Brcko.
The northern town of Brcko, which lies on a strategic corridor linking Serb-held territory in western and eastern Bosnia, is considered one of the country's most dangerous flashpoints.

Bosnia's 1995 peace accord left the future status of Brcko unresolved and international arbitration postponed a final decision until next year, appointing a U.S. diplomat to supervise the town in the meantime.

Moslems and Croats, who formed a majority in Brcko before the war, were expelled by conquering Serb forces at the onset of the Bosnian war in 1992 and Serb authorities have since blocked their return.

Foley said OSCE staff discovered identification documents which appeared to have been recently printed but were dated prior to August 1996, a cut-off date for displaced people to claim residence for voter registration.
Fraudulent registration papers claimed displaced Serbs were living in areas of Brcko heavily damaged by fighting, where there are no habitable buildings, he said.
Some applicants admitted under questioning that they had just got off a bus from neighbouring Yugoslavia and could not describe the houses or neighbourhoods of Brcko where they were registered.
Others, rejected by a registration centre for a lack of documents, would return after a few hours later with "proper" documentation, Foley said.
"Brcko is extremely sensitive and of course, it's essential that the OSCE exerts the maximum effort to protect the electoral process in this area," he said.
